A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, despite the change from TabPFN-RL to ICR-RL. Their complete text, equations, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original classic-control experiments against DQN, context-truncation comparisons and hyperparameter ablations, with experimental details in its appendix.

after.justification: v2 reports original control experiments, expanded baseline comparisons, resource analyses, backbone comparisons and ablations in the main text and appendices.

M1.justification: The central Bellman-refitting procedure, epsilon-greedy interaction and high-return gate survive under the ICR-FQI/ICR-RL names. Changes are limited to additional TabICL/TabFlex backbone instantiations and the stated RV partitioning rule: v1 targets B/2 transitions per group, whereas v2 defines groups using median episode return. The broader regression-oracle framing does not establish a redesigned algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate CartPole-v1, MountainCar-v0 and Acrobot-v1. v2 explicitly evaluates CartPole without reward shaping in Figure 6, but v1 already mentions preliminary sparse-reward experiments without identifying their environments. It is therefore unclear whether this adds a test scenario or reports previously explored coverage more fully.

E2.justification: The principal comparison expands from DQN alone to DQN, PPO and TRPO. Appendix D and Figure 10 additionally evaluate KNN, TabICL and TabFlex against the TabPFN implementation. The context-management comparator set is retained. Appendix A's descriptive comparison table does not establish experimental evaluation of its other listed methods.

E3.justification: The reported FQI budget changes from 60 iterations in v1 to approximately 10 in v2, using alpha=0.1, gamma=0.99 and K=alpha/(1-gamma). Fixed initial random batches of 200/200/128 transitions are replaced by one initial episode with epsilon=1. v2 also introduces normalized runtime/reward comparisons across context budgets and matched-hyperparameter backbone testing. These reported changes do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds context-management comparisons across memory budgets and execution times, a controlled backbone comparison without reward shaping, and sensitivity to FQI iteration count. These investigate efficiency, prior dependence and iteration-related degradation beyond v1's analyses. The original exploration, gating and context-size ablations remain; moving exploration plots to Appendix C is not an added analysis.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 3 adds uncertainty bands to the context-management comparison that v1 Figure 2 displayed as lines alone. Their statistical meaning remains unspecified. The stated ten seeds for main comparisons and five seeds per ablation setting are retained; an increase in repeated runs is not established.

E6.justification: v2 adds results for the expanded comparator set, TabICL's advantage on unshaped CartPole, context-budget/runtime tradeoffs and the finding that alpha=0.1 performs best in the iteration ablation. Main MountainCar learning curves also change between v1 Figure 1 and v2 Figure 2. Given the revised reported settings, these curves do not establish a same-setting performance improvement.

T1.justification: v2 introduces a formal risk-minimization definition of in-context regression and adds Bellman-contraction/convergence reasoning under expressivity and coverage conditions. The original Bellman updates remain, while prior-mismatch reasoning is condensed and relocated. Neither version supplies a new convergence proof for the proposed implementation.

C1.justification: The central contribution broadens from a TabPFN-specific gradient-free RL framework to a general reduction from RL to regression foundation models. The abstract and introduction expand comparison claims to PPO/TRPO, and the conclusion asserts that advances in general-purpose regression models can translate into improved RL foundation models.

C2.justification: v2 explains undiscounted episode selection as preserving delayed successes, interprets backbone-dependent performance through differing priors, and recommends fewer FQI iterations despite convergence-based expectations. These extend the interpretation, while the principal limitations concerning low-dimensional evaluation, reward shaping, prior mismatch and quadratic context costs persist.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds PPO/TRPO implementation sources and optimization hyperparameters, and documents exploration phases and iteration control. Software versions, hardware, reward-shaping formulas and reward perturbation largely carry over. Configuration details for KNN and alternative backbones remain limited, and no new code or data access information is supplied.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around regression foundation models versus RL-specific pretraining. It adds discussions of ICQL and behavioral foundation models, a comparative properties table, and references supporting alternative backbones, FQI, representation learning and adaptation. The RL2 description changes from LSTM-based to GRU-based, and several earlier references are removed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and concluding narrative are extensively rewritten around the regression-to-RL reduction. Methods are reorganized into ICR-FQI, online interaction and context engineering; prior mismatch moves into Discussion. Numbered sections and Appendices A-D replace the earlier structure, alongside the title and terminology changes.

P2.justification: The document switches from two columns to one and adds a framework diagram, comparison table and several experimental displays. Existing plots are enlarged or redrawn. The original four-panel ablation figure is split between Figures 7 and 9, including reuse of the context-size plot. These are substantial visual and organizational changes.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support beyond v1's DQN-only comparison. Policy-gradient and KNN comparisons, alternative backbones, iteration sensitivity and measured context/runtime tradeoffs address important gaps in comparative validity and the efficiency rationale. Clearer method organization also helps. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: evaluation remains concentrated on classic control, some new protocols and uncertainty bands are underexplained, and the broader foundation-model claims remain only partially tested.
